85.title: The cave of Hira
85.hook: near forty, he climbs to a small cave on a mountain above Mecca to think and pray alone
85.howItsDone: Some Muslims keep a spiritual retreat, i'tikaf, staying in the mosque in the last ten nights of Ramadan; some pilgrims to Mecca climb Jabal an-Nur to see the cave of Hira, though it is not part of the rites.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Black Stone on a cloak, and every clan lifting together. Your line was everyone takes a corner.

He has a good life now: a loving wife, children, a solid business, a name everyone trusts. Tradition says he's nearing forty. And something keeps pulling him out of town. Outside Mecca there's a steep, rocky mountain. Near the top, tucked between boulders, is a cave. Tiny: room to sit, maybe to lie down, not much more. That's where he starts going. Alone, carrying food and water up the mountain, staying days and nights at a time. Not to escape his family; he keeps coming back to them. But to be somewhere quiet enough to think.
screen: `A GOOD LIFE, NEARING FORTY.` → `A STEEP MOUNTAIN, A TINY CAVE.` → `DAYS AND NIGHTS, ALONE.`

segments.voice: The cave is called Hira. The mountain is known today as Jabal an-Nur, the Mountain of Light. The account comes down in a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. Before revelation came, she says, he began to have dreams that came true, clear as the break of dawn. Then, in her words as they've come down, solitude was made dear to him. He would worship in the cave of Hira for many nights, come back to Khadijah for more provisions, and go again. The hadith's word for it is tahannuth, and it explains the word itself: worship, night after night, a kind of spiritual retreat. What exactly he prayed, and how, the sources don't say. They tell us where, and for how long, and that he kept going back. Ibn Ishaq adds that he spent a month there every year, that the month was Ramadan, and that he fed the poor who came to him. Remember the city he was pulling away from: the valley of idols and caravans from day seventy-eight. Up there, none of it. Wind, rock, stars, and the city small below. People still climb to Hira today: a hard climb, rough steps cut into the mountain, and at the top a narrow gap in the rocks. It isn't part of any required ritual. People go because he went, and because everything that comes next in his life, and in the life of Islam, starts in that small, quiet place.

segments.voice: If you can, go a few steps higher or further away, another room, a stairwell, a parked car, the far corner of a park, and sit for two minutes where nobody needs you. Let the noise of the day get small below you, the way Mecca did from the mountain; you don't need to think of anything holy. If you pray, you can simply sit with Allah, without asking for anything.
Hira, the cave on the Mountain of Light above Mecca, where he went to be alone and pray, night after night.
Your line: go up to the quiet. Tomorrow, the night everything changes. Day eighty-five, done.

86.title: "Read" in the cave
86.hook: alone in the cave, he is seized by the angel Jibril, who says one word: read
86.howItsDone: Muslims remember the first revelation during Ramadan, especially in the last ten nights when many seek Laylat al-Qadr; many children learn Surah Al-'Alaq as one of their first surahs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hira, a tiny room of rock above Mecca. Your line was go up to the quiet.

A night in Ramadan. He's in the cave, alone, as on so many nights. Suddenly, he isn't alone. Someone is there, the angel Jibril, though he doesn't know that yet, and the angel says one word. Iqra. Read. Recite. He answers honestly: I am not a reader. He had never learned to read or write. The angel takes hold of him and squeezes him, hard, until he can't bear it, then lets go. Read. I am not a reader. Again the crushing grip. Read. Again: I am not a reader. A third time. And then the angel speaks the words he is to recite.
screen: `A NIGHT IN RAMADAN.` → `IQRA. READ.` → `I AM NOT A READER.`

segments.voice: These are the first words of the Qur'an to come down, according to most Muslim scholars. They open Surah Al-'Alaq, the ninety-sixth. In Pickthall's translation: “Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot. Read: And it is thy Lord the Most Bountiful Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not.” The first word of revelation is a command to read, given to a man who could not read. Iqra comes from the root q-r-', to read, to recite aloud, and from that root comes the word Qur'an itself: the recitation. So the first word already names the whole book. Then: in the name of your Lord. Not read anything, anyhow. Read in the name; that's the bismillah from day one of this path, now as the very first instruction. Then who He is: the one who creates, who made the human being from a clinging clot, from almost nothing. And then, twice, the pen: the one who teaches by the pen, who teaches the human being what he did not know. A man who couldn't write is given, as his first revelation, a verse about writing and learning. Muslims have taken that seriously for fourteen centuries: libraries, schools, the careful copying of the Qur'an by hand, the idea that seeking knowledge is part of faith. The Qur'an says it came down in the month of Ramadan, on a night it calls Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, better than a thousand months.
screen: `THE FIRST WORDS TO COME DOWN.` · `IQRA AND QUR'AN: ONE ROOT.` · `IN THE NAME OF THY LORD.` · `WHO TEACHETH BY THE PEN.` · then, large: `READ, IN THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Take one line that matters to you, a verse, a poem, a sentence from a letter, or today's: read, in the name of thy Lord who createth. Read it once at normal speed, then again far slower, one word at a time, letting each land before the next, and notice what you missed the first time. If you pray, you can begin with bismillah, as the first revelation did.
Iqra. Read, or recite: the first word of the Qur'an to be revealed, from the same root as the word Qur'an itself.
Your line: read, in the name. Tomorrow, he runs down the mountain. Eighty-six days now.

87.title: "Cover me"
87.hook: he runs home trembling, and Khadijah wraps him up and reminds him who he is
87.howItsDone: Muslims often quote Khadijah's words, that Allah would never disgrace one who keeps family ties and helps the weak, to encourage someone who is afraid, and honor her as the first to believe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, iqra: the first word of the Qur'an, spoken in a cave to a man who couldn't read. Your line was read, in the name.

Down the mountain he comes, his heart pounding so hard the hadith remembers it. Rough ground, loose stones, a long way home. Whatever happened up there, he has no words for it yet. No explanation, no story. He's afraid something has happened to him. He comes into Mecca, through the door of his house, straight to Khadijah, and says it over and over. Zammiluni, zammiluni. Cover me. Wrap me up.
screen: `DOWN THE MOUNTAIN.` → `HIS HEART POUNDING.` → `ZAMMILUNI: COVER ME.`

segments.voice: The hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah, says they wrapped him up until the fear left him. Just that: a blanket, and someone holding it around him. No questions yet. Then he tells Khadijah everything, and says: I'm afraid for myself. Listen to her answer. Never. By Allah, Allah would never disgrace you. Then she gives her reasons, and every one is about how he treats people. You keep up your family ties. You carry the burdens of the weak. You give to those who have nothing. You honor your guests. You stand by people when disaster hits them. He comes home terrified that something is wrong with him, and she doesn't argue theology or explain the angel. She reminds him who he is, from the evidence of how he's lived: Allah does not abandon a man who lives like that. The picture of a man wrapped up stays in the Qur'an itself. Two surahs, the seventy-third and seventy-fourth, open by addressing the Prophet ﷺ as the one wrapped up, al-muzzammil, and the one enfolded in a cloak, al-muddaththir. A hadith in Bukhari ties the second of those openings to a later day, when he came home shaken again and asked to be covered. In this story, the first comfort comes not from a scholar or a crowd, but from a wife at home, holding a blanket and telling him who he is.

segments.voice: Think of someone who's rattled right now: a scare at the doctor, a bad week, a shock they haven't told anyone about. Skip the speech and plan the blanket first, sitting with them, a meal, a call where you just listen, then two or three true things about how they've lived that you could remind them of. If you pray, you can ask Allah to steady them.

88.title: Waraqa the old cousin
88.hook: Khadijah takes him to her elderly, blind cousin, a man who knew the earlier scriptures, and the old man recognizes what came to him
88.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Waraqa in the opening chapter of Sahih al-Bukhari, and it is often told to show that the Prophet's message was recognized as belonging to the line of Musa and the earlier prophets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cover me: Khadijah wrapped him up and reminded him who he was. Your line was Allah would not disgrace you.

When something happens that nobody can explain, there's a kind of person worth finding. Not the loudest one in the room: the oldest one, who's read the most. The grandmother who's seen everything. The professor who's retired but still answers the phone. Once her husband has stopped shaking, Khadijah takes him to see her cousin. His name is Waraqa. He's very old. He's gone blind. And he has read the scriptures that came before.
screen: `WHO DO YOU GO TO?` → `KHADIJAH'S OLD COUSIN.` → `BLIND, AND DEEPLY READ.`

segments.voice: The same hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells it. Waraqa ibn Nawfal had turned away from the idols of Mecca long before and become a Christian. He could write in Hebrew, and had copied out from the Gospel as much as Allah willed. Khadijah says: cousin, listen to what your nephew has to say. The old man asks: nephew, what did you see? And the Prophet ﷺ tells him everything: the cave, the grip, the word. Read. The old blind man recognizes it at once: this is the Namus that Allah sent down to Musa. The Namus is the hadith's word for the angel who carries revelation, the keeper of the divine secret; Muslims understand it as Jibril. So Waraqa doesn't hear something new and strange. He hears something old: the same messenger who came to Musa. Then he says something heavy. I wish I were young. I wish I could be alive when your people drive you out. The Prophet asks, surprised: will they drive me out? Yes, Waraqa says. No one has ever brought what you've brought without being opposed. If I live to see that day, I will stand with you with all my strength. But, the hadith says, not long after, Waraqa died. He recognized what had come, blessed it, warned of what was coming, and was gone. Muslims remember him warmly, as a man who knew the earlier scriptures well enough to know what he was hearing.

segments.voice: Think of the oldest person you know, or the one who's read or lived the most, a grandparent, a neighbor, a retired teacher, someone at your place of worship, and pick one question you'd truly want them to answer. Picture asking it, then just listening to the whole answer without interrupting. If you pray, you can ask Allah to bless your elders.

89.title: The morning brightness
89.hook: after a painful pause in revelation, Surah Ad-Duha comes: your Lord has not forsaken you
89.howItsDone: Surah Ad-Duha is short, and some Muslims recite it in times of sadness; some also pray a voluntary prayer called duha in the bright part of the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Waraqa, the old blind cousin who recognized the messenger of Musa. Your line was the old ones recognize.

After the cave, after iqra, after Waraqa, the hadith says, the revelation paused. Nothing came, and the reports don't agree on how long. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari remembers another silence: two or three nights when he was unwell and did not rise to pray, and a woman who taunted him that his companion seemed to have left him. Silence, and then mockery about the silence. The surah that answered it is today's.
screen: `AFTER WARAQA, A PAUSE.` → `TWO OR THREE NIGHTS, AND A TAUNT.` → `YOUR COMPANION HAS LEFT YOU.`

segments.voice: Then it comes: Surah Ad-Duha, the ninety-third. In Pickthall's translation: “By the morning hours And by the night when it is stillest, Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee.” Ad-duha is the bright part of the morning, when the sun is well up and the day is fully warm. And the surah swears by two things together: the full light of morning, and the still night. As if to say: the night was real, and quiet, and that quiet was not abandonment. The morning comes after it, as sure as the sun. Then, gently: what comes later will be better for you than what came before, and your Lord will give you until you are content. Then it reminds him of his own life. Did He not find you an orphan, and shelter you? Find you wandering, and guide you? Find you in need, and enrich you? You heard the first of those on day eighty, with Halimah. You were never left before, and you aren't left now. The surah ends by turning the comfort outward: don't be harsh with the orphan, don't turn away the one who asks, and, in Pickthall's words: “Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse.” Speak of the good you've been given. Some Muslims turn to this surah in the dark stretches of their own lives: after a loss, in depression, when prayer feels like shouting into an empty room. It doesn't deny the night. It swears by it. And then it says: morning.

segments.voice: Sit in the light for a minute: a window or the open air by day, a lamp by night, or just the memory of the last morning light you felt on your face. With your eyes closed, think of one silent stretch in your life that turned out not to be abandonment. If you pray, you can recite the opening: by the morning hours, and by the night when it is stillest.

90.title: The first believers
90.hook: a wife, a boy, a freed slave and a best friend are the first to believe
90.howItsDone: Muslims honor the Prophet's earliest companions and ask Allah to be pleased with them when their names are mentioned; the first believers' stories are taught to children as examples of courage and loyalty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ad-duha, the morning brightness: after a silence, your Lord has not forsaken you. Your line was you have not been forsaken.

Before there are crowds or history books, there's a kitchen table: a few people who say yes when saying yes looks a little crazy. Islam started like that. No announcement in the marketplace, no crowd at the Ka'ba. Just a man telling the people closest to him what had happened in the cave, and watching their faces. Who believed first? Tradition names four people, and they're nothing alike.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF PEOPLE IN A ROOM.` → `NO ANNOUNCEMENT, NO CROWD.` → `WHO BELIEVED FIRST?`

segments.voice: First, Khadijah, the one who wrapped him up and said Allah would never disgrace him. Then 'Ali, his young cousin, Abu Talib's son, a boy of around ten who had been living in the Prophet's household. Then Zayd ibn Harithah. Kidnapped as a child and sold as a slave, Zayd ended up in Khadijah's house, and she gave him to her husband. When Zayd's father finally found him, years later, and came to buy him back, the Prophet ﷺ said: let him choose. Zayd chose to stay. The Prophet freed him and raised him as a son. And then Abu Bakr, his close friend, a respected merchant. Ibn Ishaq reports that the Prophet said everyone he invited hesitated at least a little, except Abu Bakr, who accepted at once. Abu Bakr then spoke to his own friends, and Ibn Ishaq names several early Muslims, 'Uthman among them, who came in through him. Muslims don't all tell the order the same way. One Sunni way of putting it: Khadijah first; among free men, Abu Bakr; among children, 'Ali; among freed slaves, Zayd. Shi'a Muslims emphasize 'Ali as the first male believer. Look at them together: a wife, a child, a freed slave, a best friend, and not a single powerful man of Quraysh. Ibn Ishaq says that for about three years the community stayed small and quiet, meeting privately, praying in secret. The Qur'an later honors as-sabiqun, the ones who went first: those who believed before it was easy, when there was nothing to gain.

91.title: Bilal on the hot sand
91.hook: an enslaved man is tortured under a rock in the midday sun, and says only one word: One
91.howItsDone: Muslims honor Bilal as the first mu'adhdhin, and many mosques and schools are named for him; his word, ahad, is remembered as a picture of steadfast tawhid.

segments.voice: Yesterday, as-sabiqun, the first believers. Your line was the first ones matter. Today ends week thirteen.

Midday in Mecca, in summer, when the sand burns through your sandals. An enslaved man named Bilal is dragged out and laid on his back. His owner has a huge rock placed on his chest, so he can barely breathe, and says: you'll stay like this until you die, or until you deny Muhammad and worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza. Bilal can't move. He can hardly draw breath. And over and over, all he says is one word. Ahad. Ahad. One. One.
screen: `MIDDAY, BURNING SAND.` → `A ROCK ON HIS CHEST.` → `AHAD. AHAD.`

segments.voice: Bilal ibn Rabah was born into slavery in Mecca; his mother was from Abyssinia, across the Red Sea. His owner, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, was one of the chiefs of Quraysh, and the biography by Ibn Ishaq tells the scene you just heard. Why that word? Ahad, One, is at the heart of a short surah, the hundred and twelfth, in Pickthall's words: “Say: He is Allah, the One!” Tawhid, day ten of this path, squeezed into a single word by a man with one breath to spend. It's quiet defiance, too: his owner owned his body, but not that word. And the story doesn't end on the sand. Abu Bakr came by, saw what was being done, bought Bilal from Umayyah and set him free. Years later, when the Muslims needed someone to call the people to prayer, they chose Bilal's voice. The first adhan, day fifteen of this path, when you first heard a word from him, was called by the man who had once said Ahad under a rock. Early Mecca was cruel to the powerless who believed. A woman named Sumayyah, tortured with her family, was killed for her faith; Muslims remember her as the first martyr of Islam. Her son 'Ammar, under torture, said what his tormentors demanded, and came to the Prophet ﷺ in tears. And the Qur'an says that one who is forced, while his heart stays firm in faith, is not blamed. Islam honors Bilal's courage, and it does not demand that everyone be Bilal. That closes week thirteen: a cave, a word, a blanket, an old cousin, the morning light, as-sabiqun, and one word on the burning sand.
screen: `BORN INTO SLAVERY IN MECCA.` · `SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE!` · `FREED, AND THEN THE FIRST ADHAN.` · `COURAGE HONORED, NOT DEMANDED.` · then, large: `AHAD, AHAD.`

segments.voice: Rest a hand flat on your chest and press gently, enough to feel it as you breathe. Choose one word to hold on to: if you pray, Bilal's word, ahad, One; if not, a word you want to keep when things push on you, like steady, or true, or someone's name. Say it silently with each breath, against the gentle weight of your hand.
Ahad, One: the single word Bilal repeated under the rock on the burning sand, refusing to deny it.
Your line: ahad, ahad. Tomorrow, the believers flee across the sea to a just king. Thirteen weeks on the path.
